items.title: September 2026 CPI: Inflation Hits 3.7% in a Tough Print for Housing
items.description: Affordability , Data , Economic Coverage , Housing Finance , Market Outlook September 2026 CPI: Inflation Hits 3.7% in a Tough Print for Housing By Jake Krimmel Oct 14, 2026 September’s consumer price index came in hotter than forecasters expected. Headline inflation rose to 3.7% year over year, and core, which had been cooling since May, ticked back up to 2.6%. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped 11 basis points within 15 minutes of the release, a sign that markets are reading this report as a preview of what’s to come. That matters for mortgage rates, which have already climbed 74 basis points since late August. Here’s what today’s report means for the Fed, consumers, and the housing market. September 2026 CPI at a Glance Headline CPI: +0.6% MoM Seasonally Adjusted (SA), following August’s +0.4% rise, versus forecasts of +0.5%; annual rate rose to 3.7% , up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% forecast Core CPI (less food energy): +0.3% MoM (SA), matching August; annual rate rose to 2.6% , up from 2.4% in August after falling from 2.9% in May Gasoline: +9.1% MoM (SA), +34.2% YoY, accounting for over half of the month’s total increase Shelter: +0.4% MoM (SA) after +0.3% in August, with rent up 0.2% and owners’ equivalent rent up 0.3%; +3.2% YoY Mortgage rates: Freddie Mac’s 30-year rate stood at 7.4% as of last week, up 74 basis points from 6.66% in late August Market reaction: the 10-year Treasury yield rose 5 basis points immediately after the release and 11 basis points within the first 15 minutes September CPI: hotter than expected, and core is no longer cooling Today’s September Consumer Price Index report came in slightly hotter than expected, with overall inflation at 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, compared to forecasts of 0.5% and 3.6%. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in the month, accounting for over half of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, also surprised to the upside, rising 0.3% month over month and up 2.6% year over year from 2.4% in August. The uptick in core, which had been trending down from 2.9% in May, is more worrying. Some CPI reports seem backward looking and stale, while others seem like they’re foreshadowing what’s to come. This one definitely feels like the latter. We are in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory when it comes to the next Fed rate increase. What it means for the Fed: a hike is a matter of when, not if Still, today’s firmer numbers are probably not enough to change the Fed’s holding bias in October, especially given the dovish talk from New York Fed President John Williams earlier this week . But a hold is hardly the slam dunk it was earlier. Today’s numbers all but guarantee a hike by December though, while further opening the door for one or more hikes in early 2027. We are in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory when it comes to the next Fed rate increase. Bond markets noticed too, with the 10-year Treasury yield up 5 basis points immediately and 11 basis points in the first 15 minutes after the release. The evolution of bond yields and hike odds are two key things to monitor for mortgage rates this week and next. What it means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers This is a tough print for housing, not because of what higher inflation means for right now but because of what it may mean moving forward. Freddie Mac mortgage rates went from 6.66% in late August to 7.4% as of last week , a 74 basis point rise that is good for a 7.2% loss of purchasing power, or over $22,000 in house price for a buyer with a $2,000 monthly principal and interest budget. Given these numbers, it’s no surprise that housing demand has been hit hard. NAR existing home sales fell 2.2% year over year in September, while Realtor.com data show pending sales down 4.1% and new contract signings down 9.8%, both leading indicators for where closed sales are headed in the coming months. Sellers are slashing prices too, with 20.8% of listings

items.title: Fannie Mae slashes 2027 mortgage forecast amid higher rates
items.description: Fannie Mae ’s Economic and Strategic Research Group cut its 2027 mortgage origination forecast by 18% in its October outlook, signaling that mortgage rates are expected to stay higher and refinance volume will remain weak. The ESR Group now projects total single-family originations in 2027 will reach $1.86 trillion, down from $2.27 trillion in its September forecast. For this year, Fannie Mae economists still expect about $2 trillion in volume. Higher rate assumptions are driving the downgrade, with the Federal Reserve (Fed) expected to continue raising interest rates — the next Federal Open Market Committe e meeting concludes Oct. 28. Fannie Mae now expects 30-year mortgage rates to average 7.5% in 2026, up from 6.7% in the September outlook. Refinance activity takes the brunt of the revision. Fannie Mae now expects 2027 refinance originations of about $430 billion, roughly half of the prior $802 billion estimate and below the approximately $695 billion projected for this year. Purchase originations are forecast to total $1.4 trillion in 2027, essentially flat with this year, underscoring that the market will remain purchase-driven. On the macroeconomic front, the ESR Group kept its outlook for real gross domestic product growth at a 2.5% increase, suggesting the weaker mortgage outlook is more about rates than recession risk. Inflation expectations edged higher, with the Consumer Price Index now projected to rise 1.9% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2027, compared with 1.7% in the prior forecast. Feeling the strain “Rates have gotten higher than what anybody expected, compared to where people were expecting things to be six months ago,” said Gagan Sharma, founder and CEO at BSI Financial . “What is that manifesting itself? Servicing is more expensive than it ever has been, origination has been harder but the economy is doing great actually.” Fannie Mae’s view differs somewhat from that of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), which also assumes elevated rates and subdued volume but with its own trajectory. The MBA’s baseline forecast released during their annual convention this week in Chicago calls for 30-year mortgage rates to remain above 7% through 2027, after reaching 7.5% last week. At those levels, MBA economists expect total single-family mortgage originations to decline 5% to $1.99 trillion in 2027, down from $2.1 trillion projected for 2026. For MBA economists, that backdrop points to more consolidation among independent mortgage banks. “At the height in 2021, we were at about 881 companies (independent mortgage banks), and that’s now down to 707 at the end of 2025 – so, that doesn’t even account for what’s happened this past year,” Marina Walsh, vice president and head of industry analysis at the MBA, said. She added, “There has been a movement toward consolidation. I do think that M A activity may continue, especially if companies feel like they have to make big investments, big technology investments and they’re not capable of doing that. But if they join forces with another company that has the capital, has the cash to do so, it would make a lot of sense.” Related More: Fannie Mae Mortgage Rates

items.title: Build-to-rent communities now eligible for FHA financing
items.description: Politics and policy Build-to-rent communities now eligible for FHA financing By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 15, 2026, 4:56 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content What's at Stake: Whether the new FHA financing will actually lower rents or expand housing supply. Expert Quote: "It does not alter real-world bottlenecks" — Thom Malone, principal economist, Cotality Supporting Data: Fewer than 100,000 annual starts for one specific property type. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Build-to-rent lending, a property type exempted from the ownership restrictions in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, got a boost from the Department of Housing and Urban Development on Wednesday. If anything, the Act was expected to create a shift among business-purpose lenders away from single-family rental transactions towards BTR properties. Some BPL originators acquire their production through the correspondent channel. These properties are now eligible for Federal Housing Administration-insurance under two multifamily programs: Section 221(d)(4) for new construction and Section 223(f) for acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental communities. "In theory, this announcement will lower the cost of capital for BTR by providing more stable and cheaper financing options," said Thom Malone, principal economist for Cotality. "This would increase the supply of rental housing, which would put downward pressure on rents, but that would be blunted since it would also increase demand by making more families choose renting over buying." However, Malone thinks the effects would be extremely small, possibly not even detectable in practice. "Even if the cost of capital is lower, it does not alter real-world bottlenecks like processing delays and restrictive local zoning," Malone continued. BTR is not a large part of the market, he said, with the number of starts totalling fewer than 100,000 a year. "Even if this program increased that by 20%, that would still mean only 15,000 to 20,000 more rental units — a drop in the bucket of the U.S. rental market," Malone said. Still, this change not only helps those who need this type of financing but also gives lenders another product they can offer at a time when industry economists are expecting owner-occupied residential volume to decline 5% in 2027. HUD Secretary Scott Turner. Photographer: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg "America needs more affordable housing," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release. "We're eliminating barriers to spur development, expand rental options and improve housing affordability for hardworking American families." While a fair amount of investor-property loans goes through the non-agency market, certain non-owner occupied premises are eligible for government-sponsored enterprise financing. The Community Home Lenders of America, whose membership consists of single-family originators who concentrate on the owner-occupied segment, still sees this announcement as having a broader impact on housing. "We need an 'all hands on deck' approach to our nation's affordable housing challenges," Scott Olson, the group's executive director, said. "So while this does not directly affect homeownership — CHLA's top priority as the trade group exclusively representing non-bank single-family lenders — housing is a continuum, and this is a very constructive action, which CHLA supports, to develop more affordable rental housing." Build-to-rent communities typically consist of single-family homes, duplexes or triplexes. Under the change, FHA insurance will cover both site-built and manufactured home BTRs and treat them under the same terms and conditions as traditional multifamily rental developments. items.title: Surging jobsite raids put 370,000 new home completions at risk
items.description: America’s homebuilders entered the fall with 256,000 newly constructed homes still under construction for sale and another 114,000 permitted or otherwise classified as not yet started. Together, those 370,000 homes represent an enormous amount of work builders still have to complete, along with intensifying business risk tied to their ability to do so. The figures come from the Census Bureau’s August New Home Sales report, as highlighted by housing economist Bill McBride of Calculated Risk . They take on added urgency as builders enter the final months of 2026, racing to move homes through the remaining stages of construction, complete deliveries before winter and year-end, and convert invested capital back into cash. These are homes for sale, not homes already under contract. But that distinction should not be mistaken for a lack of financial exposure. By the time a builder has secured land, developed lots, obtained permits, and committed to a speculative home, the builder has already invested capital and assumed risk. For the 256,000 homes under construction, those commitments are substantially further along. Many of those homes are approaching the point where a reliable sequence of finishing trades determines whether a project closes on schedule or slips into another month, quarter, or year. Drywall installers, painters, flooring crews, finish carpenters, and other subcontractors must arrive in the right order, with little room for delays. That’s where a serious problem has taken hold in the homebuilding landscape. Just as homebuilders need to complete work already underway, the skilled trade crews required to finish those homes are becoming harder to secure. Immigration enforcement is adding another layer of disruption to an already constrained workforce , threatening construction schedules, increasing carrying costs and putting additional pressure on businesses whose margins and cash flows are already stretched. It would be one thing if immigration enforcement were merely reducing the availability of construction workers. What’s now becoming clear is that an industry already struggling to sell homes may be unable to reliably finish the homes it has invested so much upfront capital in. A labor shortage in a slowing housing market Normally, slower homebuilding activity would ease competition for construction workers. With fewer new starts, builders should have more flexibility to secure the crews needed to complete projects already underway. But residential construction does not operate in isolation. Skilled workers and subcontractors can pursue opportunities in commercial construction, infrastructure, and the rapidly expanding data-center sector , where demand for certain trades remains strong. As a result, a slowdown in new-home production does not necessarily translate into greater labor availability for homebuilders. Immigration enforcement is now ratcheting up that squeeze. The combination is particularly dangerous at this point in the construction and business cycle. Builders are entering the final weeks of the year with significant capital tied up in homes at various stages of completion. Many are trying to complete projects before winter weather complicates schedules and before year-end financial and delivery targets come due. A shortage of framing crews can delay a project early in its timeline. A shortage of drywall installers, painters, flooring specialists, or finish carpenters can prevent a nearly completed home from being delivered, even after most of its construction costs have already been incurred. A home that is 90% complete is not 90% of a closing. Until the remaining work is finished, inspections are passed and a buyer can take possession, the builder may be unable to realize the expected sales proceeds. items.title: Existing Home Sales Point to a Slow Market Despite Uptick
items.description: Economic Coverage , Existing Home Sales Existing Home Sales Point to a Slow Market Despite Uptick By Danielle Hale Oct 13, 2026 September 2026 existing-home sales Existing home sales ran at a 3.99M pace in September, 2.2% behind the September 2025 pace (4.08M) but up 1.5% from their August pace of 3.93M which was revised down from the initially reported tally (3.98M). Mortgage rates climbed in July and remained near 6.7% in August when these closed sales likely went under contract, which likely helped the market regain some momentum in September. While 6.7% looks like a good mortgage rate given that the market is well-above 7% today , in early August this rate was a 2026 high and the first time in 44 weeks that mortgage rates had surpassed their prior year level which is why we see a decline from last year. Home sales are likely to remain below their year-ago pace for the rest of 2026 as mortgage rates remain high. The month to month pickup NAR’s pending home sales steadied in August dropping just (0.3%) from July, but trailed the prior year by a larger gap (-4.7%). Meanwhile, Realtor.com September pending home sales also dropped by a larger margin , signaling a rough patch for existing home sales. After a rapid repricing in the second half of September, the 10-year yield has hovered in a narrower 5.2% to 5.3% range in the last two weeks, a stability that will eventually help to stabilize mortgage rates and rebuild homebuyer confidence for navigating the market, but this takes time. Rising Inventory and Slower Sales Keep Months Supply Elevated After climbing to 4.9 months in August, its highest pace since November 2015 (5.1), months supply was revised to 4.8 months, a mark it held in September, amid lower inventory and lower sales. Realtor.com data show that even though new listings remained sluggish in September , not topping their prior year pace as was common in the spring, active inventory continues to rise. First-time Home Buyers Gain Ground First-time home buyer share edged higher, building on gains last month. In September, first- time home buyers purchased 31% of sales, up from 30% in the prior month and year. We’re past the worst of the starter-home supply crunch nationwide, which may help entry-level buyers gain a foothold, but the local picture remains mixed according to the latest Realtor.com report. Home Prices Rose Modestly Home sales prices rose 1.3% from the prior year even as they slipped lower on a monthly basis, as is typical seasonally. The typical U.S. asking price has been softer in 2026 according to Realtor.com data, lagging behind by 1.4% in September .

items.title: Chicago Office Tower Sells For $550M To Zara Founder In Blockbuster Deal
items.description: Chicago Office Tower Sells For $550M To Zara Founder In Blockbuster Deal October 14, 2026 | 6:23 pm ET Ryan Wangman, Chicago Amancio Ortega , the founder of the fashion retailer Zara , reportedly acquired the 51-story office tower at 1 N. Wacker Drive for about $550M, one of the priciest office deals in the country this year. Wikimedia Commons/TastyPoutine 1 N. Wacker Drive in Chicago Irvine Co . sold the more than 1.4M SF office property to Ortega's family office in a deal Tuesday that includes the assumption of a $353M CMBS loan Irvine took out in 2021, CoStar News first reported . The sale hadn't been posted in Cook County property records as of Wednesday evening. Only two larger full-building office trades occurred nationwide in 2026: the $730M sale of Park Avenue Tower in New York City, which closed in January, and the $691M sale of the Transamerica Pyramid in San Francisco in April. In Chicago, the deal is the largest outright office sale since the Aon Center sold for $712M in 2015. It is the highest valuation since 100% of the equity interest in the Bank of America Tower sold for $210M in March 2022, a deal that put the tower's implied value at more than $1B. The 51-story tower at 1 N. Wacker was completed in 2001 and is about 94% leased to a tenant roster that includes PwC , UBS and Fitch Ratings , according to CoStar. Ortega's real estate investment arm, Ponte Gadea, is no stranger to the city, making another major splash in Chicago when it dropped almost $232M on the 492-unit apartment tower at 727 W. Madison St. in 2023. This is the first time Irvine Co. has exited a Chicago property, CoStar reported. It still owns two other trophy office towers in the city: 71 S. Wacker Drive and 300 N. LaSalle St. The deal for 1 N. Wacker has been in the works for months, with Irvine Co. reportedly beginning to shop the property as early as January. Cushman Wakefield Managing Director Jeff Skender said at last month's Bisnow Chicago lease conference that he was interested in a 1 N. Wacker sale because the property has top-of-the-market rates and minimal vacancy. "The question to owners is: OK, you're trying this hard to maintain your face rates. What is the reward in this capital markets environment on that reversion when you bring that to market?" Skender said at the end of September. "And I think 1 N. Wacker is going to be a really good test of that." items.title: Build-to-rent now eligible for Federal Housing Administration financing
items.description: An article from Dive Brief Build-to-rent now eligible for Federal Housing Administration financing Under the policy change, BTR projects can qualify for new construction and acquisition or refinancing programs, as HUD pushes to increase housing supply. Published Oct. 16, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Kent Nishimura via Getty Images Listen to the article 3 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: Build-to-rent housing is now eligible for Federal Housing Administration-insured financing through two of its multifamily mortgage insurance programs, according to an announcement from HUD. The update is effective immediately. Multifamily rentals that consist of single-family homes, duplexes or triplexes, including site-built and manufactured, will now be treated under the same terms and conditions as traditional multifamily rental developments. The shift reflects the “expanding presence of professionally managed” build-to-rent communities and the growing demand for them, per the release. HUD’s update applies to FHA's Section 221(d)(4) program for new construction as well as its Section 223(f) program for acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental communities, according to a mortgagee letter that outlines eligibility criteria . Dive Insight: Historically, the Office of Multifamily Housing limited its insured loans to developments with buildings containing four or more units, according to the letter. “BTR properties were excluded due to their single-family design and subdivision-style layout that raised concerns about Fair Housing Act compliance (particularly, accessibility design requirements) and valuation and underwriting challenges,” the letter reads. The FHA’s policy change aims to make it easier to finance new rentals and increase the overall housing supply, “particularly in light of manufactured housing innovation,” according to the release. Production of manufactured housing has dwindled from its peak in the 1970s and 1980s, with the drop in production due in part to HUD’s 1974 permanent chassis mandate that added up to $10,000 to the development cost of a new unit, Smart Cities Dive reported. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , which became law in July, updated manufactured housing regulations and eliminated that chassis requirement. Now HUD plans to explore new manufactured housing designs that can be built quickly. To qualify for FHA funding, BTR properties must be developed on a single uninterrupted site and operated as a single property and in a similar fashion to other multifamily projects on the market, per the mortgagee letter. Projects consisting of a mix of multifamily housing, with a BTR component along with traditional apartment buildings, are permitted. Although manufactured or modular construction is allowed, the agency does note that these methods “add challenges to HUD’s traditional approach to insuring advances for work installed on-site, and these issues must be carefully vetted at the concept meeting,” according to the mortgagee letter. Expanding the overall rental housing supply is key to improving affordability, according to Joe Gormley, who oversees the FHA and Office of Housing. “Combined with other initiatives we are working on at HUD, including chassis removal in our manufactured housing programs, we are unshackling the market to deliver housing where it’s needed most,” Gormley said in the release. items.title: TMG, KKR Acquire San Jose's Skyport Plaza from Hudson Pacific
items.description: California CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. California + Bay Area + Office | October 16, 2026 By: Paul Bubny TMG, KKR Acquire San Jose’s Skyport Plaza from Hudson Pacific TMG Partners has acquired Skyport Plaza, a 435,000-square-foot office and retail complex located at 1650 Technology Dr., 1700 Technology Dr., 50 Skyport Dr. and 90 Skyport Dr. in San Jose. TMG Partners acquired the asset together with accounts managed by KKR. The seller was Hudson Pacific Properties, which announced a $75.5-million sale price. In conjunction with the acquisition, TMG signed a long-term, 393,000-square-foot lease with the County of Santa Clara. The 30-year lease is expected to commence in the first quarter of 2029, following extensive renovations to the two office buildings, formerly occupied by Qualcomm and now 100% vacant. The retail is fully occupied. “We’re pleased to support the County of Santa Clara in their consolidation at Skyport Plaza which will provide a more efficient and modern experience for their employees,” said TMG co-CEO Ben Kochalski. “We look forward to working with them on the property improvements to modernize the infrastructure for their staff, as well as provide a location where they can conveniently access services and restaurants.” Read More News Stories About: KKR Connect Inside The Story About Paul Bubny Paul Bubny serves as Senior Content Director for Connect Commercial Real Estate, a role to which he brings 19-plus years’ experience covering the commercial real estate industry and 35-plus years in business-to-business journalism. In this capacity, he oversees daily operations while also reporting on both local/regional markets and national trends, covering individual transactions across all property types, as well as delving into broader subject matter. He produces 11-15 daily news stories per day and works with the Connect team and clients to develop longer-form content, ranging from Q As to thought-leadership pieces. Prior to joining Connect, Paul was Managing Editor for both Real Estate Forum and GlobeSt.com at American Lawyer Media, where he oversaw operations at both publications while also producing daily news and feature-length articles. His tenure in B2B publishing stretches back into the print era, and he has served as Editor in Chief on four national trade publications. Since 1999, Paul has volunteered as the newsletter editor of passenger rail advocacy groups (one national, one local). items.title: Lenders Accuse Nord Group Entities Of Pocketing Rents, Faking Insurance As Multifamily Empire Crumbles
items.description: Lenders Accuse Nord Group Entities Of Pocketing Rents, Faking Insurance As Multifamily Empire Crumbles October 15, 2026 | 6:59 pm ET Maddy McCarty, Houston Magistrate Judge Andrew Edison had run out of patience. He had just heard arguments from attorneys for Freddie Mac , which had foreclosed on a 228-unit apartment complex in Lake Jackson, Texas, claiming that the property's previous owner was still collecting rents. The owner, a subsidiary of New York-based Nord Group , had stopped making mortgage payments 18 months earlier. But it nevertheless sued its lender over alleged breach of contract, eventually claiming that it still legally possessed the property after foreclosure due to a technicality. Edison wasn’t amused, calling the behavior “pretty damn egregious.” “I mean, come on,” Edison said during a May 26 hearing. “The property has been foreclosed. Get out of the damn property. Stop taking money that doesn't belong to you.” A fed-up federal judge is just one of a host of issues piling up for Nord Group and its 27-year-old CEO and co-founder, Saqif Noor. Instagram/Saqif Noor Saqif Noor in an Instagram post shared Oct. 22, 2023 Lenders and investors have accused Nord entities of stealing rents, providing fake insurance records and keeping buildings in an “alarming state of neglect that poses serious health, safety and habitability concerns.” Court filings detail hazards including sewage backups, mold, vermin and cat feces rendering apartments unlivable. Nord Group is one of many investors that spent heavily on apartments in the ultralow-interest-rate environment of 2021 and 2022, but its collapse stands out for the apparent deception behind its buying spree and the rapid deterioration of its properties. Investigators are circling, and Nord's 11-property portfolio built between 2021 and 2023, fueled by nearly $400M in largely government-backed debt, is slipping out of its grasp. In phone calls in February and April with an investor, recordings of which were shared with Bisnow , Noor said he signed for his father on loan documents, that the FBI has questioned his former partner, and that he’s pretty sure he will spend time behind bars. “I think camp time is inevitable. It’s inevitable. It’s going to happen,” Noor said on the call. “Prison time. Camp sounds a little nicer.” In an email to Bisnow , Noor denied these conversations took place. His former partner, Baruch Teitelbaum, denied being questioned by the FBI. When presented with a detailed list of questions, Noor wrote, “A lot of the info here on your email seem to be baseless false,” and referred comment on Nord litigation to his attorney. Noor didn't respond to follow-up questions. Nord Group and its subsidiaries have been party to at least two dozen lawsuits, bankruptcy cases and appeals since late 2023, according to hundreds of pages of court records reviewed by Bisnow . Numerous cases have been dismissed or halted by bankruptcy proceedings, but at least five remain open, including litigation with Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae and lawsuits from residents who allege negligence resulting in the drowning of a child and a man being shot. A Nord entity denied responsibility in the drowning case. Nord Group never responded in the shooting case, filed last October, and this week was ordered to pay a $6.6M default judgment to the alleged victim. “The Nord Group provides housing for thousands of working-class Americans and is proud of their role in the communities they serve,” Nord's attorney, Jason Kraus, said in a statement. “We cannot comment on any pending court cases and will not litigate through the media, but please understand that mere allegations in lawsuits are just that — allegations specifically drafted to inflame, gain media attention and are not proven facts. The Nord Group of companies vigorously denies all allegations and will continue to defend itself in court.” Noor started Nord Group with backing from his father, Dr. Khaled Noor, and in partnership with Teitel

items.title: Beazer Homes stockholders approve $2.2B sale to Dream Finders
items.description: The stockholders of Beazer Homes overwhelmingly approved the Dream Finders Homes ’ pending acquisition of Beazer at a special meeting held earlier this week, moving the deal closer to closing, the companies announced on Thursday. The stockholder vote is one of the final remaining conditions for the transaction. The parties previously received early termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act, and Dream Finders said it expects to complete the deal on Oct. 20, 2026, using previously disclosed available or committed financing sources. Under the terms of the all-cash transaction. first announced in August, Dream Finders will acquire Beazer at an enterprise value of approximately $2.2 billion. Beazer shareholders will receive $33.50 in cash for each share of Beazer common stock, implying a purchase price-to-book value multiple of 0.8x. Beazer is a national homebuilder operating in 15 markets across 13 states. Once the acquisition closes, Dream Finders and Beazer are expected to form what the companies describe as the nation’s sixth-largest homebuilder by volume, with complementary geographic footprints and expanded product offerings. The combined platform will operate in 26 markets and approximately 520 active communities across the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, Texas, the West and the Midwest mdash; regions that include many of the country’s highest-demand housing corridors. This larger footprint will increase the company’s reach across both entry-level and move-up communities, positioning the combined builder to serve a broader buyer base across multiple price points. They also expect to realize purchasing efficiencies and operational scale that could support more competitive pricing and a more streamlined homebuying experience. items.title: Terra Lands $507M Loan For Miami Beach Condo Tower: The South Florida Deal Sheet
items.description: Terra Lands $507M Loan For Miami Beach Condo Tower: The South Florida Deal Sheet October 12, 2026 | 6:30 pm ET Chloe Gallivan, South Florida David Martin's Terra and a trio of partners landed one of the largest construction loans of the year for their planned condo project in Miami Beach. Google Maps The site of the project at 1250 West Ave. in Miami Beach Terra, RG Development Group, GV Development and Lore Development landed a $507M construction loan from Tyko Capital , according to a release. The deal is among the largest to ever hit South Florida, following Related Ross ' $772M construction loan last year for two office towers in West Palm Beach and the $668M construction loan Property Markets Group landed in 2024 for the Waldorf Astoria Hotel Residences Miami. The joint venture is planning a 28-story, 106-unit condominium building at 1250 West Ave. with private wellness and recreational amenities, a spa and a padel court. Plans also include underground parking and ground-floor retail. Terra teamed up with JDS Development , led by Michael Stern , to purchase all of the units of the 61-year-old condo tower on the site for $120M in September 2025, but JDS is no longer involved with the project, a Terra spokesperson confirmed to Bisnow . Northwind Group lent JDS and Terra $98M to finance the buyout. The change-up in the lineup comes as Stern faces a handful of lawsuits over his other Miami projects. Stern's Mercedes-Benz condo project is facing an $80M foreclosure suit , and Fontainebleau Development 's Jeff Soffer is in talks to partner on the project as Stern works on $1B in financing, The Real Deal reported . Stern is also in a back-and-forth with GV Development's Gianluca Vacchi, who joined forces with JDS in 2024 to invest in a $4B development pipeline, including 1250 West Ave. GV Development filed a second lawsuit against the developer in July, claiming that Stern was diverting new investments into other projects and his own projects. PEOPLE JLL hired three office brokers from Avison Young to its Fort Lauderdale office, according to a release. Avison Young's founding partner of Florida operation, Greg Martin, principal Justin Cope and office leasing broker Lisa Blumer landed new roles with JLL to expand its agency leasing and landlord representation team across Broward and Palm Beach counties. Martin and Cope were named senior managing directors, and Blumer was named senior vice president. Martin has 30 years of experience in commercial real estate, with a focus on Class-A and B office leasing, and Cope has been in the South Florida commercial real estate scene for 20 years and specializes in Class-A office leasing and landlord representation. Blumer has more than 10 years of experience and specializes in office agency leasing and landlord advisory. LEASES Terra landed a 40K SF lease with Walmart for a small-format store at Doral Atrium, the latest project in a fast-growing Miami retail construction pipeline . The lease brings the 78K SF development to 95% leased as Walmart joins tenants like PNC Bank, Bonchon Chicken, Sushi Mas, Tremble Pilates and The Good Feet Store. There is roughly 8K SF left available for lease. Doral Atrium shopping center is on the northwest corner of Doral Boulevard and 79th Avenue.
